title: Rook against pawn
summary: The cut-off, the rook behind, counting, the shoulder and the right check; on the pawn's side, the king in front, the knight, the corner, the staircase and the rook that draws against the queen.
part.cutting.title: The cut-off
part.cutting.summary: The rook builds a wall between the black king and the pawn, on a rank or on a file, and the pawn is left alone.
part.behind.title: Rook behind the pawn
part.behind.summary: When you cannot cut the king off, the rook goes behind the pawn: it only moves with its king alongside, and your king walks around the outside.
part.counting.title: Counting the tempi
part.counting.summary: No cut-off and no shortcut: you count. The king walks diagonally, towards the squares in front of the pawn, and one tempo decides.
part.shoulder.title: The shoulder
part.shoulder.summary: When both kings race to the same place, your king steps into the other one's way and keeps it far from the pawn.
part.check.title: Checking with tempo
part.check.summary: The rook checks to drive the black king out of the way; the check that pushes it in front of the pawn throws the win away.
part.pawnKing.title: Kamsky versus Bacrot
part.pawnKing.summary: With the pawn, the king walks in front of it and blocks the other king's path: Bacrot's defence against Kamsky, Sofia, 2006.
part.knight.title: Knight promotion
part.knight.summary: On the pawn's side: when a queen would be mated, the knight is born with check and sticks to its own king.
part.knightTrap.title: No hurry with the king
part.knightTrap.summary: On the rook's side: first the rook behind the pawn, then the king, away from the squares where a knight gives check.
part.stalemate.title: The saving corner
part.stalemate.summary: On the pawn's side: with a knight's or rook's pawn on the second rank, the king goes into the corner, and capturing the pawn is stalemate.
part.staircase.title: The king's staircase
part.staircase.summary: The king walks down a staircase towards the rook, avoiding the pin and the skewer, until the pawn queens: from Fenton–Potter, 1875, to the Saavedra position.
part.fortress.title: Rook against queen
part.fortress.summary: When the pawn is going to queen no matter what: the rook protected by its king checks without end or trades itself for the queen. And the rules to take into the practical challenge.
step.t_cut: The d4-pawn is on its own, and your king is far away, on h7. The black king, on f6, is one step from touching the pawn. If your king walks straight there, it arrives late. Which rook move gains the time you are missing?
step.t_cut.hint1: The black king is not glued to the pawn yet. Can you stop it from getting there?
step.t_cut.hint2: Look for a whole rank that the black king has to cross to reach the pawn.
step.d_cut: Rook against pawn is a race: the pawn walks on its own, but the rook needs its king to win. If your king arrives in time, the pawn falls; if it arrives late, it is a draw. Here your king is far away, on h7, and the first tool for gaining time is the cut-off: the rook builds a wall on the fifth rank, and the pawn is left alone on the other side.
step.d_cut.m1: 1.Ra5! The whole fifth rank is now off limits for the black king. It can no longer come down to the pawn.
step.d_cut.m2: 1...Ke6: the black king looks for a way down the e-file, but the wall is still there.
step.d_cut.m3: 2.Kg6: your king joins the race. Now every move of yours counts, because the pawn is on its own.
step.d_cut.m4: 2...Kd6: it tries the other side, and stays stuck above the fifth rank.
step.d_cut.m5: 3.Kf5: your king is already on the rank of the wall, two steps from the pawn.
step.d_cut.m6: 3...Kc6: the black king has nothing to do. If the pawn runs, the rook goes to the d-file and captures it on its own.
step.d_cut.m7: 4.Ke4: your king has reached the pawn, and it falls next move. The cut-off cost one move and won the race.
step.fileCut: The wall can also be a file. Here the black king wants g6 and g5, next to the pawn, and your king on d8 wants the pawn. 1.Rf2+ forces the black king off the f-file, and the rook stays on it: a wall between the king and the pawn. It can no longer cross to the pawn's side.
step.fileCutMove: Cut off along the file, with check, and then take your king to the pawn.
step.fileCutMove.hint: 1.Rf2+ The black king leaves the f-file and does not come back. Then 2.Ke8, towards the pawn.
step.fileCutMove.done: The black king is left on the wrong side of the wall, and your king goes via f8 or f7 to fetch the pawn. In the exercises you will make this cut-off with the colours reversed.
step.t_behind: Now the black king is close to the c5-pawn, and your king is in the corner, on a8. No rank or file separates the black king from the pawn. Where does the rook work best?
step.t_behind.hint1: If the rook cannot drive the black king away, can it at least force it to stay tied to the pawn?
step.t_behind.hint2: Think of the squares the pawn still has to step on: who protects them if the black king walks away?
step.behindIdea: You cannot always cut the king off: here nothing separates the black king from the pawn. So the rook goes behind the pawn, 1.Rc8! It stops the pawn from moving without an escort: at every step, the black king has to stand next to it to defend it. And while the black king looks after the pawn, your king gains the tempi it was missing.
step.d_behind: The same idea with your king close by, in a training position by Ezryn. With the rook on c8, the black king has to escort the pawn through c4, c3 and c2; your king does not force its way through, it walks around the outside and reaches the pawn when it is on the second rank. Ezryn calls it outflanking.
step.d_behind.m1: 1.Rc8: behind the pawn. Now c4 can only come with the king next to it, or the rook captures.
step.d_behind.m2: 1...c4: the black king stays next to it, as an escort.
step.d_behind.m3: 2.Kc7: your king does not step into the black king's way; it walks around the outside.
step.d_behind.m4: 2...Kd4: the black king protects c3, the pawn's next square.
step.d_behind.m5: 3.Kb6: one more step around the outside. The black king cannot leave the pawn's side.
step.d_behind.m6: 3...c3: another step with an escort; the pawn only moves because the king is glued to it.
step.d_behind.m7: 4.Kb5: your king has reached the pawn's side. Then 4...Kd3 5.Kb4 c2 6.Kb3, and the pawn falls on c2 with no way forward.
step.behind: Rook behind the pawn, then the king on its way.
step.behind.hint: 1.Rc8, behind the pawn. Then the king comes: 2.Ka7.
step.behind.done: Rook behind the pawn and king on its way. The black king has become the pawn's nanny, and your king will arrive before the pawn queens.
step.t_count: Now no cut-off works: the black king is next to the f4-pawn, and your king is far away, on b7. Only one move wins, and it is a king move. Which way does it go?
step.t_count.hint1: Count: how many moves does the pawn need to reach f1? And your king, to get close to it?
step.t_count.hint2: Which squares does your king need to reach: the ones behind the pawn or the ones in front of it? The king walks diagonally as fast as in a straight line.
step.race: You count. The pawn needs three moves to reach f1. Your king has to arrive in time to help the rook win the pawn. The shortest way is diagonal, towards the squares in front of the pawn, e3 and e2, not behind it: 1.Kc6! Lose one move and the sums no longer add up.
step.d_count: Watch the sums add up: three pawn moves, three king moves.
step.d_count.m1: 1.Kc6! Diagonally, towards the squares in front of the pawn. Any other move is already late.
step.d_count.m2: 1...f3: the pawn runs, and two moves remain before it queens.
step.d_count.m3: 2.Kd5: another diagonal. The king aims at e3 and e2, the squares beside the pawn's path.
step.d_count.m4: 2...Kf4: the black king protects the pawn from behind and takes e3 away from your king.
step.d_count.m5: 3.Kd4! Just in time, next to e3. Now the pawn cannot pass f2 without being caught.
step.d_count.m6: 3...f2: one step from queening, but the white king is already beside its path.
step.d_count.m7: 4.Rf1: the rook stops the pawn. It cannot move any more, and your king goes to e3 and e2 to collect it.
step.late: The same position with your king one square further away, on c8. Now the sums do not add up: whichever way it goes, your king arrives one move later than needed, and the black king escorts the pawn to the end. It is a draw. In this ending a single tempo decides everything. That is why you count before you play.
step.count: Back to your king on b7. Make the sums add up, move by move.
step.count.done: Three pawn moves, three king moves: your king reached the side of e3 just in time, and the rook goes to f1 to stop the pawn.
step.t_shoulder: Sometimes both kings race to the same place. The black king, on e3, wants to reach d3 and d2, next to the c4-pawn; your king is on e6. Which king move keeps the black king away from the pawn?
step.t_shoulder.hint1: Which squares does the black king need to reach the pawn?
step.t_shoulder.hint2: Your king does not need to touch the black king: it is enough to take the squares on its way, ideally while attacking the pawn.
step.bodycheck: When both kings race to the same place, push with your shoulder. The black king wants to reach d3 and d2, next to the pawn. With 1.Kd5! your king steps into its way: it takes the squares the black king needs, and the black king is left outside, far from the pawn. That is the shoulder: your king pushes the other one away without touching it.
step.d_shoulder.m1: 1.Kd5! Attacks the pawn. If 1...Kd3, touching it, 2.Rh3+ drives the king away and the pawn falls; so Black's best is to run with the pawn.
step.d_shoulder.m2: 1...c3: it runs, but the black king is still far from d3.
step.d_shoulder.m3: 2.Kc4! The square d3 is gone for the black king, and the pawn is attacked again.
step.d_shoulder.m4: 2...c2: the last step before queening, with no escort.
step.d_shoulder.m5: 3.Kc3: the black king never got near the pawn. Next move, 4.Kxc2 or 4.Rc1, and the pawn falls.
step.shoulder: Put your king in the black king's way and stay there.
step.shoulder.hint: 1.Kd5, attacking the pawn. After 1...c3, 2.Kc4, which takes d3 from the black king. After 2...c2, 3.Kc3.
step.shoulder.done: The black king never got near the pawn. Your king stood between them, and the rook finishes the job.
step.t_check: 1.Rh5+ is free: the black king has to leave e5. Is that check worth giving?
step.t_check.hint1: Where does the check send the black king? Closer to the pawn or further from it?
step.t_check.hint2: Who reaches the squares in front of the pawn, d3 and d2, first? Remember the tool from the second chapter: the rook can force the black king to escort.
step.checkIdea: A check costs the black king a move, but that move may be useful to it. Look at 1.Rh5+? The king goes to e4 or f4: towards the pawn, exactly where it wanted to be, with your king behind. That does not gain time, it loses it. What wins is 1.Rd8! The rook stays behind the pawn, the black king has to escort, and your king walks around in front.
step.d_badCheck: Watch what happens after the wrong check, 1.Rh5+?
step.d_badCheck.m1: 1...Ke4: the black king goes in front of the pawn, which now moves with an escort.
step.d_badCheck.m2: 2.Kd6: your king comes, but the black king is already on e4, ahead of it and glued to the pawn.
step.d_badCheck.m3: 2...d3: every pawn step is protected by the king.
step.d_badCheck.m4: 3.Rh4+ Another check, and another useful move for Black.
step.d_badCheck.m5: 3...Ke3: the black king stays glued to the pawn, one square ahead of your king. It reaches d2 before you do: a draw. The check gave the black king the square it wanted.
step.d_goodPlan: Now the rook behind, without a check.
step.d_goodPlan.m1: 1.Rd8! Behind the pawn. Now d3 can only come with the black king next to it.
step.d_goodPlan.m2: 1...Ke4: the black king escorts the pawn, because without it d3 falls to the rook.
step.d_goodPlan.m3: 2.Kd6: your king heads for the squares in front of the pawn; with the rook behind it, the pawn cannot move without the black king beside it.
step.d_goodPlan.m4: 2...d3: with an escort; the black king is tied to the pawn's side.
step.d_goodPlan.m5: 3.Kc5: closer. The black king cannot leave the pawn to push yours away.
step.d_goodPlan.m6: 3...Ke3: it protects d2, the pawn's next square, and has no time for anything else.
step.d_goodPlan.m7: 4.Kc4: your king has reached the squares in front of the pawn. After 4...d2, 5.Kc3, and the pawn falls; if 5...d1=N+, 6.Rxd1 captures the knight.
step.tempoGood: And when does a check gain time? When it drives the black king away from the front of the pawn. Here the black king is on e3, ready to escort the pawn, and your king on f7 cannot arrive in time. 1.Re8+ forces the king off the e-file: on the d-file it stands in front of its own pawn and blocks it; on the f-file it moves away. Either way, the rook goes back behind the pawn with 2.Rd8. That one move is exactly what your king needed.
step.check: Give the tempo-gaining check and bring the rook back behind the pawn.
step.check.hint: 1.Re8+ After 1...Kf3, the rook goes back behind the pawn: 2.Rd8.
step.check.done: The check moved the black king away from the front of the pawn. Now it needs a move to come back, and in that move your king walks around and arrives.
step.t_pawnKing: Now the pawn is yours. You are Bacrot, with Black, against Kamsky, in Sofia, 2006: the white king has just captured your rook with 66.Kxh7, and what is left is the e5-pawn against the rook. Which square does your king need to occupy first?
step.t_pawnKing.hint1: The pawn's king walks in front of it, not behind it.
step.t_pawnKing.hint2: Block the white king's path to the pawn with your king, and only push the pawn when the white king is far away.
step.pawnKingIdea: Mtel Masters, Sofia, May 2006, second round. Kamsky has just captured the rook with 66.Kxh7, and Bacrot is left with a pawn against the rook. The position holds the draw, but every black move, from 66...Kd3 to 74...e1=N+, is the only one that holds. Three things guide the defence: the king in front of the pawn, not behind it; the king blocking the white king's path, which is the shoulder seen from the pawn's side; and the pawn only moves when the white king cannot attack it.
step.d_bacrotDef: Watch how Bacrot defended, move by move.
step.d_bacrotDef.m1: 66...Kd3! The king goes in front of the pawn on the d-file side, away from the rook. On e3 it could not use the f-file, cut off by the rook on f8, to block the white king's path: after 66...Ke3? 67.Kg6 the white king arrives in time.
step.d_bacrotDef.m2: 67.Rd8+ Kamsky checks to drive the king away from the pawn.
step.d_bacrotDef.m3: 67...Ke3! The only move. The rook has left the f-file, so e3 now works: the king stays in front of the pawn, protects e4, its next square, and takes d4 and f4 away from the white king.
step.d_bacrotDef.m4: 68.Kg6: the white king comes, but d4 and f4 are still off limits to it.
step.d_bacrotDef.m5: 68...e4! Now, while the white king is two squares away and cannot attack the pawn. The black king covers d3 and f3.
step.d_bacrotDef.m6: 69.Kf5: Kamsky attacks the pawn with his king. One of your exercises starts here: the next black move blocks the white king's path.
step.robson: Five years later Robson had the same ending against Bacrot, at the 2011 World Cup in Khanty-Mansiysk, and this time Bacrot had the rook. Robson held with accurate moves up to here and played 87...h2?? He lost: after 88.Rg6+ Kh3 89.Kf2 the white king reached the pawn; then came 89...h1=N+ 90.Kf3 Kh2 91.Rg7, and the knight in the corner has nowhere to go, because every square of its is covered by the king or the rook. The saving move was 87...Kg2! The king shuts f2 to the white king, the shoulder of the side with the pawn, and after 88.Rg6+ goes to f1, next to the pawn.
step.pawnKing: Now you are Robson. Hold the draw: block the white king's path.
step.pawnKing.hint: 87...Kg2! Takes f2 from the white king. After 88.Rg6+, 88...Kf1, glued to the pawn.
step.pawnKing.done: The black king shut f2 and stands on f1, next to the pawn. The white king cannot get in, and the rook alone cannot win the pawn: the king goes back and forth between g2 and f1, and it is a draw.
step.t_knight: Still on the pawn's side: yours is on e2, one step from queening. But the white king has reached d3, and the rook on a2 is waiting for the queen to be born to mate on the first rank. The goal is to draw. How?
step.t_knight.hint1: After 1...e1=Q, what does the rook play?
step.t_knight.hint2: Look for a move that forces White to answer before giving mate.
step.d_knight: The queen is born and dies: 1...e1=Q? 2.Ra1, mate. The knight is born giving check, and that gains the tempo. Watch the knight save the game.
step.d_knight.m1: 1...e1=N+ Check. The rook cannot mate because the white king has to move first.
step.d_knight.m2: 2.Kc3: the king steps out of check and stays close, hoping to capture the knight.
step.d_knight.m3: 2...Nf3! The knight leaves the white king's reach and stays one jump from e1 and d2, close to its own king.
step.d_knight.m4: 3.Rf2: the rook attacks the knight and tries to separate it from the king.
step.d_knight.m5: 3...Ne1: back to the king's side. The rook cannot capture it, because the king defends it.
step.d_knight.m6: 4.Rf1: the rook attacks the knight again, now along the rank.
step.d_knight.m7: 4...Ke2: the king defends the knight and moves away from the white king. Rook and king cannot separate the two: a draw.
step.knight: Notice what saved you: 1...e1=N+! The knight was born giving check to the king on d3, and White lost the move for the mate. Afterwards the knight sticks to its own king, and the rook cannot separate them: it is a draw. Whoever defends with the pawn has to know this resource; whoever has the rook has to avoid falling for it.
step.knightMove: Your turn: save the draw with the pawn.
step.knightMove.hint: 1...e1=N+, with check. After 2.Kc3, 2...Nf3, away from the white king and one jump from your king.
step.knightMove.done: The knight was born with check and stayed close to your king. Rook and king cannot separate the two: a draw.
step.t_trap: Now the rook's side. The d2-pawn is one step from queening, with the black king on d1, in front of it, and your king on f2, very close. It looks like time to bring the king nearer, but remember the knight. Which move wins without giving it a chance?
step.t_trap.hint1: If the pawn becomes a knight on d1, on which squares does it give check?
step.t_trap.hint2: Before moving the king, the rook can attack the pawn from a square the pawn cannot escape.
step.rushWhy: White wins with any rook move along the eighth rank, 1.Rd8 for instance, behind the pawn. What throws the win away is hurrying the king: 1.Ke3? It looks natural, bringing the king closer, but e3 is exactly the square on which a knight born on d1 gives check. Watch the punishment.
step.d_rush: The white king rushed to e3. Now
step.d_rush.m1: 1...Ke1! The black king leaves the pawn's file and frees d1 for the promotion.
step.d_rush.m2: 2.Rh8: the rook threatens 3.Rh1, mate, and seems to decide the game.
step.d_rush.m3: 2...d1=N+ The knight is born giving check on e3, exactly the square the king rushed to. The white king has to move, and the mate on h1 never comes.
step.d_rush.m4: 3.Kd3: the white king tries to stay close to the knight to capture it.
step.d_rush.m5: 3...Nf2+ The knight escapes with another check and stays close to its king. Rook and king cannot corner it: a draw. The hurry cost the win.
step.trap: The same position, before the mistake. Win without giving the knight a chance.
step.trap.hint: Do not move the king yet. 1.Rd8, behind the pawn. After 1...Kc2, 2.Ke2, and after 2...Kc3, 3.Rxd2.
step.trap.done: The rook attacked the pawn from behind and the white king arrived via e2, where no knight check gains anything. First the rook, then the king.
step.t_stalemate: You have the b2-pawn. The rook has just attacked it along the second rank, and the white king protects b2. The pawn is going to fall. Where does your king go so that it does not matter?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Think of a position in which, after the rook captures the pawn, your king has no move at all.
step.t_stalemate.hint2: After 2.Rxb2, which squares do the rook and the white king cover? Look for the square where your king has no way out.
step.stalemateIdea: 1...Ka1! Now, if the rook captures the pawn, 2.Rxb2, the black king has no move: a2 and b1 are covered by the rook, b2 by the white king. It is stalemate, a draw. And if the rook does not capture, it cannot get the king out of the corner. It is the typical knight's-pawn draw on the second rank: the king in the corner, next to the pawn.
step.d_stalemate.m1: 1.Rd2: the rook attacks the pawn along the second rank, and the white king protects b2.
step.d_stalemate.m2: 1...Ka1! The king goes into the corner, next to the pawn. It wants to be left without moves.
step.d_stalemate.m3: 2.Rxb2: White captures the pawn, and Black has no move at all. Stalemate, a draw.
step.rookPawnCorner: With a rook's pawn the corner saves you too. The a2-pawn is one step from queening, and White checks with 1.Rb8+. The king goes to a1, in front of its own pawn: the rook cannot capture the pawn without stalemating, and the king goes back and forth between a1 and b1. If the white king comes as close as c3 with the black king on a1, it is stalemate just the same.
step.d_rookPawn: Watch the corner with the rook's pawn.
step.d_rookPawn.m2: 1...Ka1! Into the corner, in front of its own pawn. Capturing the pawn now would be stalemate.
step.d_rookPawn.m3: 2.Ra8: the rook attacks the pawn along the file, and the black king has to leave the corner, but it stays glued to the pawn.
step.d_rookPawn.m4: 2...Kb1: the king leaves the corner; if the rook captures the pawn now, the king captures the rook. And if 3.Rb8+, back with 3...Ka1. White makes no progress.
step.stalemate: The pawn is going to fall. Make it not matter.
step.stalemate.hint: 1...Ka1: the king in the corner, next to the pawn. If the rook captures, it is stalemate.
step.stalemate.done: The king without moves is the defence. Capturing the pawn stalemates; not capturing makes no progress.
step.t_staircase: Now the pawn is yours, and it is one step from queening. The rook has just checked with 1...Rd6+, and a pin and a skewer are lurking. Where does the king go?
step.t_staircase.hint1: Towards the rook, one rank at a time.
step.t_staircase.hint2: 2.Kb7? Allows 2...Rd7, which pins the pawn. 2.Kc5? Allows 2...Rd1, and after the promotion comes 3...Rc1+. Avoid both.
step.staircaseIdea: G. E. Barbier published this position in 1895, recalling a game from twenty years earlier; the technique is Kling and Horwitz's, from 1853. The king walks down a staircase towards the rook: 2.Kb5, 3.Kb4, 4.Kb3. With every check it goes down one rank, and the rook cannot follow it down forever: on d3 it is already within reach of 5.Kc2. Two wrong paths. 2.Kb7? Allows 2...Rd7, pinning the pawn. 2.Kc5? Allows 2...Rd1, the rook waiting for the queen to be born on c8 so it can play 3...Rc1+ and skewer it.
step.d_staircase.m1: 2.Kb5! One step down, towards the rook. Neither b7 nor c5.
step.d_staircase.m2: 2...Rd5+ The rook comes down too and checks again.
step.d_staircase.m3: 3.Kb4: another step down, always on the b-file, beside the rook.
step.d_staircase.m4: 3...Rd4+ Another check, and the rook is already one rank from the king.
step.d_staircase.m5: 4.Kb3: now the rook has only one check left, on d3, and there it is within the king's reach.
step.d_staircase.m6: 4...Rd3+ The last possible check, because the rook on d3 is already within the king's reach.
step.d_staircase.m7: 5.Kc2: attacks the rook. The c-file is safe now, because the rook can no longer check without being captured.
step.d_staircase.m8: 5...Rd4: the rook tries one last trick. If 6.c8=Q, then 6...Rc4+ forces the queen to capture. But notice where the black king is.
step.d_staircase.m9: 6.c8=Q: with the black king on h6 there is no stalemate after 6...Rc4+ 7.Qxc4, and the lone queen wins. With the king on a1, it would be another story.
step.fenton: The game Barbier tried to recall: Fenton against Potter, London, 1875, an informal game in which Fenton played at odds. Here he played 53.Rxh3 Kxh3 54.Kc6 Rxa5 55.b7 Ra6+ and agreed a draw, believing there was no escape from the checks. Zukertort showed the same year that White was winning: the king had to walk down the staircase towards the rook, as you have just seen, and not to the wrong side. 56.Kb5? Allows 56...Ra1! The queen born on b8 meets 57...Rb1+ and falls. The position after 55...Ra6+ is one of your exercises.
step.d_saavedra: The same staircase with the black king on a1 is the Saavedra position. Barbier published it as a draw: 5...Rd4 6.c8=Q Rc4+ 7.Qxc4, and Black is stalemated. Saavedra, a Spanish priest living in Glasgow, found the answer at move six.
step.d_saavedra.m1: 6.c8=R!! A rook instead of a queen. 6...Rc4+ no longer works, because after 7.Rxc4 the black king has moves. And the new rook threatens 7.Ra8, mate.
step.d_saavedra.m2: 6...Ra4: the only defence against mate on the a-file.
step.d_saavedra.m3: 7.Kb3! Attacks the rook and threatens 8.Rc1, mate. The black rook falls or mate follows. The pawn has beaten the rook.
step.staircase: Walk down the staircase: three steps towards the rook.
step.staircase.hint: 2.Kb5, 3.Kb4, 4.Kb3: one rank at a time, down the b-file. Neither b7 nor c5.
step.staircase.done: Three steps, and the rook has run out of useful checks: after 4...Rd3+, 5.Kc2 attacks the rook and the pawn queens.
step.t_fortress: The black queen has just been born on f1, and you only have the rook and the king. Queen against rook usually wins, but here your king on g7 is right next to the rook. The goal is to draw. Which move holds?
step.t_fortress.hint1: A rook protected by its own king cannot be captured by the black king.
step.t_fortress.hint2: If the black king never gets a free move, the queen has no time to help.
step.fortressIdea: The queen has just been born on f1 and you only have the rook. Even so, there is a draw. The rook stays on g6 or h6, always protected by the king on g7, and checks every move, starting with 1.Rg6+. The black king can neither capture it nor hide: on the g- and h-files it is checked, and if it steps onto the f-file, the rook's check on the f-file attacks the king and, behind it, the queen. Running far away loses the queen; staying next to it only allows the trade of rook for queen, and king against king is a draw.
step.d_fortress.m1: 1.Rg6+ Check, with the rook protected by the king. The black king cannot capture it.
step.d_fortress.m2: 1...Kh3: it steps out to the h-file. Its other way out, the f-file, runs into the check you will see in 4.Rf6+.
step.d_fortress.m3: 2.Rh6+ The rook jumps to its file, protected again.
step.d_fortress.m4: 2...Kg4: it comes closer, trying to reach the rook.
step.d_fortress.m5: 3.Rg6+ Back to g6. The rook alternates between g6 and h6 as long as the king stays on the g- and h-files.
step.d_fortress.m6: 3...Kf3: it steps onto the f-file, close to the queen.
step.d_fortress.m7: 4.Rf6+ The rook attacks the king and, behind it, the queen. If the king runs far away, the queen falls for free; if it goes back to e2 or g2, next to her, the rook captures the queen and the king recaptures: king against king, a draw.
step.fortress: Give the checks with the protected rook and do not let the black king breathe.
step.fortress.done: The protected rook checks without end, and the black king has nowhere to hide. That is the fortress; in the exercises you will have to prepare it.
step.recap: Three rules. One: with the rook, cut the king off or put the rook behind the pawn, and count the tempi, with the king walking diagonally and using the shoulder. Two: check only if it drives the king out of the way. Three: with the pawn, the king goes in front and blocks the path, and there are four saves: the knight with check, the corner that stalemates, the staircase towards the rook and the protected rook against the queen.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Cut off the black king or put the rook behind the pawn, count the tempi and beware of the knight.
ex.e11: This time the rook is yours, and the white pawn is still on g2. The white king wants to get close to it. Don't let it. Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: A rook can cut along a file too. Which file separates the white king from the pawn?
ex.e11.solution: 1...Rf7+. The check drives the white king off the f-file, and the rook stays there as a wall. The toughest defence is to go to the e-file, and from there it can't get back to the pawn; on the g-file, next to the pawn, it loses even faster. The pawn is left alone, your king walks down calmly and the rook wins the pawn. Any other move lets the white king reach the pawn in time, and it's a draw.
ex.e12: A rook pawn, and your king is on the other side of the board. Find the missing tempo.
ex.e12.hint: Before putting the rook behind the pawn, force the black king out of the way.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Rg6+. The black king must leave the g-file: if it goes to the h-file, it stands in front of its own pawn and slows it down; if it goes to f3, the rook gets behind the pawn with 2.Rh6 (2.Rf6+ also wins). With the pawn held, your king arrives via c5, d4 and e3. 1.Rh6 right away is one tempo late: the black king escorts the pawn and it's a draw.
ex.e13: The pawn is pinned on the second rank and the white king protects the rook. It looks hopeless. Find the saving move.
ex.e13.hint: Sometimes having no legal move at all is the best defence.
ex.e13.solution: 1...Kh1!, into the corner. If White captures the pawn with 2.Rxg2, the black king has no square and it's stalemate; if not, White can't make progress. 1...Kh3 loses the pawn to 2.Rxg2, and 1...Kg1 loses after 2.Rxg2+, with the rook protected by the king. It's the typical knight-pawn draw: the king in the corner, next to the pawn.
ex.e14: There's a free rook check. Does it help? Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: Where would the check send the black king? Think about who reaches the squares in front of the pawn first.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd6! Your king heads for the squares in front of the pawn; after 1...Ke4, the rook gets behind the pawn with 2.Rg7 (2.Re7+ also wins), and the white king comes via d5 and d4. The check 1.Rd5+ looks natural, but it sends the black king to f4, exactly where it wanted to go: in front of the pawn, with your king behind. Then it's a draw. Not every check gains time; the one that gains time is the check that moves the king out of the way. Only 1.Kd6 wins.
ex.e15: Now the pawn is yours, and the black rook is checking. Where does the king go? Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: Two traps: the pin on the seventh rank and the check on the b-file after promotion. The king has to walk towards the rook.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kc5! After 1...Ra5+, 2.Kc4; the checks go on with 2...Ra4+ 3.Kc3 Ra3+ 4.Kb2, and then they run out: the pawn promotes. The king walks down a staircase towards the rook. 1.Kb5? throws away the win to 1...Ra1: if 2.b8=Q, 2...Rb1+ and the queen falls. 1.Kc7? allows 1...Ra7, pinning the pawn, and 1.Kd5? allows 1...Rb6, winning the pawn. This is Zukertort's analysis of the game Fenton–Potter, 1875, the position the Saavedra study grew out of.
ex.e16: Kamsky–Bacrot, Sofia, 2006. The white king is coming for the pawn and the rook is ready. Defend to the end, one move at a time. Find the draw.
ex.e16.hint: First, use your king to block the white king's path. At the end, when a queen can't be born, remember there are other pieces.
ex.e16.solution: 69...Kf3!, the shoulder: the black king takes the squares the white king would walk through. After 70.Rh8, 70...e3; after 71.Rh3+, 71...Kf2; after 72.Kf4, 72...e2; after 73.Rh2+, 73...Kf1; and after 74.Kf3, 74...e1=N+!, with check. Each of these is the only move that holds. Promoting to a queen at the end loses: 75.Rh1 is mate. Rook against knight, with the knight next to its king, is a draw. In the game Bacrot found the knight, but went wrong later and lost.
ex.e17: The pawn will become a queen and nothing can stop it. Even so, there is a draw. Where does the rook need to be? Find the draw.
ex.e17.hint: Your king protects more than one square on the sixth rank. A protected rook that checks forever doesn't need to win anything.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Ra6!! After 1...c1=Q, 2.Rb6+; after 2...Ka3, 3.Ra6+, and so on, along the a- and b-files. The rook is always protected by the king on b7, and the black king can't get away: if it steps onto the c-file, the rook check on c6 puts the rook in front of the queen, which can only be saved by trading itself for the rook. Other moves lose: the queen is born and the black king escapes the checks.
key.cut: The cut-off: the rook sits on a rank between the black king and the pawn and keeps it from helping while the white king makes its way over.
key.shoulder: The shoulder: the white king steps into the black king's path and pushes it away from the squares beside the pawn.
key.check: A check at the right moment: the rook drives the black king back, and the white king gains the tempo it was missing.
key.knight: The defender's resource: promoting to a knight, with check, saves the draw. Promoting to a queen would lose.
key.saavedra: Saavedra, 1895: here the pawn beats the rook. Promoting to a queen would stalemate the black king; promoting to a rook wins.
history: Rook against pawn looks easy: a rook is worth far more than a pawn. But if the rook's king is far away and the pawn well advanced, there is often not enough time, and a single move separates a win from a draw. The most famous case is an exception: in 1895 a Glasgow newspaper published a rook-against-pawn position as a draw, and a Spanish priest living in the city, Fernando Saavedra, showed that the pawn actually won, by promoting to a rook instead of a queen so as not to stalemate the enemy king. Ever since, the Saavedra position has been one of the best-known studies in chess. In everyday games the rule is simpler: with the king close, the rook wins; with the king far away, you have to count the moves.
practice: The practical challenge: rook against pawn, and your king is far away. Count the tempi, walk diagonally and give the knight no chance. The goal is to win.
